title: From Probation to Partnership: Building Equitable Systems of Support in Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT Community colleges serve as critical gateways to higher education for diverse student populations, yet traditional academic probation systems often exacerbate inequities by penalizing students facing systemic and personal challenges. This practitioner–scholar case study examines Clark State College's Academic Engagement Program (AEP), an equity‐driven redesign of academic probation that replaces punitive frameworks with trauma‐informed, student‐centered support. Grounded in a dual GPA model, early alert systems, and technology‐enabled engagement, the AEP reframes academic distress as an opportunity for partnership and institutional accountability. Drawing on data and student feedback, this study explores how proactive coaching, inclusive language, and cross‐departmental collaboration improve retention and persistence, particularly among racially minoritized and first‐generation students. Findings reveal significant term‐to‐term GPA improvements and higher persistence rates for program participants, though persistent equity gaps underscore the need for broader institutional reform. title: Racial Equity in State Funding for Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT States vary significantly in both the amount of funding they allocate to community colleges and the mechanisms they use to distribute these funds (Kelchen et al., 2024; Mullin et al., 2015; State Higher Education Executive Officers, 2025). One major source of variation in state's approaches to funding community colleges is whether and how they incorporate race considerations in their funding models. For example, some states include weights for enrolling or graduating students with certain racial categorizations (Gándara et al., 2026). Including race‐based adjustments in funding models is one way to address the “education debt” owed to racially minoritized communities that has resulted from ideas, ideologies, and actions that have marginalized or otherwise harmed these communities (Ladson‐Billings, 2006, p. 5). Estela Bensimon (2007) developed the concept of equity mindedness to assess racialized assumptions about historically minoritized people . As Bensimon (2020), building on Ladson Billings (2006) and Kendi (2019), argues, addressing education debt requires anti‐racist policy, which includes naming race in policy. title: Racial Noticing and Community College Leaders: Implications for Equity‐Minded Organizational Change
abstract: ABSTRACT This article complexifies equity‐mindedness by adding the “how” to the concept of critical race‐consciousness, introducing racial noticing as a framework for understanding how community college leaders attend to, interpret, and respond to racial phenomena during campus equity projects (CEPs). Using a qualitative multiple‐case study design, we conducted exploratory interviews with 11 leaders from three community colleges engaged in designing and implementing campus racial equity change projects. Interviews explored leaders’ racial noticing, their perceptions of other team members’ racial noticing, and how these lenses shaped CEP development, implementation, and communication. Four attending lenses emerged: Attending to Racialized Harm, Attending to the Offending, Attending to the Potentially Resistant, and Attending to Power. Leaders attended to different racial phenomena, and these differences produced tensions during the creation and implementation of CEPs. Across the three cases, white leaders most often Attended to the Offending or the Potentially Resistant, while leaders of color were more likely, although not exclusively, to Attend to the Racially Harmed. title: The Equity‐Minded Board? Leadership, Accountability, and the Future of Community College Governance
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how community college governing boards can advance racial equity by extending Bensimon's equity‐mindedness to the level of institutional governance. Using document analysis of California Community Colleges (CCC) Board of Governors (BOG) policies and governance artifacts (2023–2025), we analyze how equity is enacted at the board level. We introduce the Equity‐Minded Governance Framework—comprising equity accountability, stewardship, and learning—to evaluate the BOG's efforts and identify gaps. Findings show strong commitments to race‐conscious planning and policy development, but limited mechanisms for trustee learning and board‐level accountability. Drawing on agency and stewardship theory, we argue that equity goals remain vulnerable to drift without explicit monitoring structures. We conclude with recommendations for embedding equity‐minded governance practices to strengthen boards’ capacity to advance racial justice.

title: Guided Toward Equity: Communities of Practice and Organizational Change in Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT Although community colleges advance equity by providing opportunities for marginalized students to pursue higher education, barriers to earning credentials remain, particularly for students of color. Higher education stakeholders are investing in “equity work” as organizations take responsibility for ensuring equitable outcomes. While ample research explores individual organizational change efforts, the impact of cross‐institutional interventions such as guided communities of practice (COPs) remains understudied. This article examines the effects of one such intervention, the Illinois Equity in Attainment (ILEA) initiative. The ILEA initiative engaged 25 colleges and universities across the state of Illinois in an effort to operationalize “equity‐mindedness” and catalyze institutional change. Drawing on qualitative case study data from three participating community colleges, we trace how guided equity planning translated into specific organizational practices, analyzing the distinct understandings of equity formed at each college, the diagnosis of inequities through the use of disaggregated data, and the development of interventions to promote more equitable student outcom

title: Connecting Students With Public Benefits: Early Lessons From Kynectors in the Kentucky Community and Technical College Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Basic needs insecurity of college students has been prevalent across the country. As a way to address this issue, there has been a recent discussion of helping students apply for and benefit from public subsidies such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Since 2024, the Kynector initiative, hiring a full‐time professional who can help students connect to government subsidies, has been implemented at all sixteen Kentucky Community and Technical College Systems. This chapter introduces the new initiative in Kentucky and provides early lessons from the initiative.

title: Equity in Context: Institutional Agency in Targeting Student Supports in Massachusetts Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT How do related, but independent community colleges operationalize and implement an equity‐oriented initiative? In 2021, Massachusetts established the SUCCESS initiative to provide nonfinancial student supports in all 15 of the state's public community colleges. This paper draws on 35 interviews with program staff across the colleges to ask how they used their institutional data and designed new data collections to (1) select a focal population for their SUCCESS program and (2) apply their criteria to identify a specific cohort. While we find variation in what the colleges viewed as their most urgent equity gaps, we find that in all colleges, data availability informed how practitioners could identify their focal students. Our findings illustrate how diverse community colleges within one state respond differently to the same equity‐oriented initiative; they operationalize equity in different ways that are related to their institutional priorities and data availability.

title: A Faculty AI Narrative: Reimagining Pedagogical Capacity in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines the integration of generative artificial intelligence into College and Career Success 1001, a first‐year experience course at a large community college in Connecticut, through a combined literature review and reflective narrative methodology grounded in traditions of autoethnography, scholarly personal narrative, and reflective practitioner inquiry. National research indicates that community college faculty are adopting AI primarily to streamline instructional tasks, enhance accessibility, and support course design, while expressing ongoing concerns about assessment integrity, student agency, privacy, and ethical implementation. Against this backdrop, I documented a year‐long exploration of AI as a pedagogical partner, using tools such as Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT, NotebookLM, and Poe to refine communication, redesign course materials, generate multimodal assignment supports, and analyze patterns in student work. The narrative highlights both the promise and limitations of AI, including challenges related to platform compatibility, variability across AI versions, and the ethical risks posed by student‐facing chatbots without guardrails. title: Faculty Commitment to Equity‐Mindedness: Development and Initial Validation of a New Measure
abstract: ABSTRACT Equity‐mindedness has become a widely adopted framework for advancing racial equity in higher education, yet little research has examined the extent to which faculty internalize equity‐minded principles as enduring professional commitments. To address this gap, this study conceptualized faculty commitment to equity‐mindedness as a distinct dimension of equity‐minded practice and developed the Faculty Commitment to Equity‐Mindedness Survey (FCEMS) to measure the construct. A complementary Equity‐Minded Implementation Contexts Survey (EMICS) was also developed to assess faculty‐reported equity efforts and perceptions of institutional and departmental support for equity‐minded work. Survey data were collected from 64 faculty members at a California community college designated as a Hispanic‐Serving Institution (HSI), who had participated in equity‐focused professional development. Exploratory factor analysis supported a two‐factor structure for the FCEMS, consisting of FCEM Values and FCEM Responsibility. The FCEMS demonstrated strong internal consistency reliability, while correlations with EMICS subscales, Equity Efforts and Perceived Support, provided initial evidence of c

title: Beyond the Classroom: How Community College Websites in Texas Communicate Dual Enrollment Information and Student Support Services
abstract: ABSTRACT Dual enrollment (DE) has expanded rapidly, yet students’ access to support services remains uneven. This study examined 55 community college websites in Texas to evaluate how clearly and comprehensively they presented DE information and communicated student support services. Using a three‐domain rubric encompassing website navigation (accessibility), presentation of DE information (usefulness), and availability of student support services, the analysis found that DE pages were generally accessible but offered limited multilingual options and inconsistent financial transparency. While most sites listed eligibility, procedures, and contacts, nearly one in five omitted cost information. Communication of student support services was the weakest area; advising was common, but orientation, wellness, and co‐curricular opportunities were far less visible or were ambiguously described. Misalignments appeared between the ease of locating DE pages and the usefulness of their content. Findings suggest that clearer, multilingual, and student‐support services‐integrated web communication can serve as an equity lever for DE participants.

title: Enacting Equity‐Minded Change with Community College Latine Students in Rural Settings: Student Voice and Federal Policy
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how Hamiter led equity‐minded change at Jupiter Valley College (JVC), a rural Hispanic‐Serving Institution (HSI), serving predominantly first‐generation college students from low‐income backgrounds who reside in a rural community in California. In doing so, this study highlights how Hamiter leveraged HSI funding as a mechanism to confront structural barriers hindering Latine students at JVC. Using a life history portal approach and equity‐mindedness as the guiding framework and analytic lens, we trace how Hamiter's role in securing and implementing an HSI grant positioned her to gather, protect, and mobilize student voice. This study advances understandings of equity‐minded policy implementation by underscoring how an HSI designation and Title V funding can support organizational change when equity‐minded practitioners use student experiences, institutional relationships, and campus structures to confront racialized barriers in rural community colleges.

title: Crossing Tuition Borders: Evaluating AB‐91 Through an Equity‐Minded Lens in California Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT California's Assembly Bill 91 (AB‐91), passed in 2023 and effective Fall 2024, authorizes nine community colleges in the San Diego and Imperial Counties region to waive nonresident tuition for low‐income Mexican national students residing within forty‐five miles of the U.S.‐Mexico border. Employing an Equity‐Minded Policy Analysis framework grounded in Bensimon's (2007) concept of equity‐mindedness, this study examines AB‐91's first‐year enrollment effects and the role of institutional capacity in shaping implementation across eligible colleges. We estimate a staggered Difference‐in‐Differences model that leverages variation in implementation timing across two waves of adoption. Results indicate a positive but statistically insignificant overall average treatment effect on Hispanic visa‐holding student enrollment, with trajectory balancing confirming minimal and inconsistent enrollment changes during the policy's initial year. Exploratory analysis of an Institutional Capacity Index suggests that while capacity did not determine implementation timing, it shaped how effectively colleges operationalized the policy once adopted. These findings underscore a persistent gap betwe

title: Building and Leading an Equity‐Minded Collective
abstract: ABSTRACT This article documents our learnings from creating and sustaining a three‐year equity‐minded collective supporting over 200 colleagues across 23 community colleges in California (Bensimon, 2005). Within our state context, all 116 campuses serving 2.1 million students create institutional documents known as “Student Equity Plans” that span three‐year cycles under the Student Equity and Achievement (SEA) program (California Community Colleges Chancellor's Office [CCCCO], n.d.). This program, in existence since the 1990s, has required colleagues to create these institutional equity plans since 2014. Each of the authors hold some experience with student equity; whether its writing these plans, spending years implementing proposed ideas within them, or studying the efficacy of them in improving outcomes for racially minoritized students (Felix, 2021). Given these experiences, the authors came together in 2021 to work collaboratively, seeking to bridge the gap between system‐level intent of policy and campus‐wide impact via implementation.

title: Civic Development of Latine Students: The Role of Equity‐Minded Community College Leaders
abstract: ABSTRACT This study explores how equity‐minded educators at Hispanic Serving community colleges (HSCCs) foster the civic development of Latine students, emphasizing leadership, civic engagement, and agency beyond academic success. Using a multi‐case study design, we analyzed interviews with 29 educators from two HSCCs in Southern California to understand their perceptions and practices. Findings show educators assume personal responsibility for developing racial literacy and critical consciousness as foundations for civic engagement. Strategies include integrating local history into curricula, building community partnerships, and creating paid opportunities for students to engage in social justice work. These efforts reflect a commitment to dismantling inequities and preparing students as agents of change. The study calls for institutionalized approaches to embed equity and civic development into policies, curricula, and professional development.

title: Equity by Design: The Equity‐Minded Digital Syllabus as a Tool for Faculty and Organizational Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT Community colleges continue to confront persistent racial inequities in student outcomes despite longstanding commitments to access and inclusion. While equity‐mindedness positions faculty as critical agents of institutional change, less is known about how instructional tools support the development of equity‐minded (EM) practice and organizational learning. This qualitative study examines the influence of an EM digital syllabus at Crown City Community College (pseudonym), a California community college that embedded EM design principles into its learning management system. Guided by Bensimon and Dowd's application of Cultural–Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), the study explores how six faculty members experienced and utilized the EM digital syllabus in their teaching. Findings suggest that the EM digital syllabus functions as a mediating artifact that supports faculty reflection, instructional redesign, and equity‐minded pedagogical practice. Participants described shifts in course design, communication, grading, and student support that moved beyond individual acts of care toward greater attention to structural equity and institutional accountability. Findings also reve

title: Student Leadership as Equity Practice: Latine Student Leaders Shaping Equity‐Mindedness in Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT This qualitative study examines how Latine student leaders engaged in equity‐oriented leadership through Avance, a student leadership initiative at a Southern California Hispanic‐Serving Community College (HSCC). Guided by Bensimon's (2007) equity‐mindedness framework, the study explores how participation in Avance shaped students’ equity‐minded perspectives, sense of agency, leadership identity, and engagement in institutional equity efforts. Findings indicate that students developed equity‐mindedness through student‐faculty partnerships, shared governance, and culturally affirming leadership experiences that fostered their capacity to recognize and address inequities within the college. Involvement in Avance also strengthened students' confidence as leaders and affirmed their cultural and linguistic identities as assets in leadership. The findings suggest that student leadership structures can serve as important mechanisms for cultivating equity‐mindedness and servingness by positioning students as partners in equity‐oriented institutional transformation.

title: Representation Matters: The Importance of Aligning Community College Student Affairs Professionals With a Growing Latinx Student Body
abstract: ABSTRACT Student affairs professionals are essential to community college student success, yet their demographic composition remains largely static in student affairs administration, failing to reflect an increasingly diverse student body, specifically the rapidly growing Latinx population. While women constitute most of this workforce, Latinx women specifically encounter significant barriers to equitable advancement and representation within leadership. Compounding these inequities is the accidental nature of the profession, where many practitioners lack formal academic preparation and the positional power to change institutional structures. Consequently, professional development pathways, ranging from national competency frameworks to applied doctoral programs, have emerged as vital paths for growth. This article provides a literature‐informed discussion on the preparation of student affairs professionals and why representation matters when it comes to employee and student success. We highlight how a lack of culturally responsive mentorship and the absence of inclusive pedagogical training among doctoral faculty can hinder effective modeling of equity principles. title: Unlocking Potential: Redefining Community College Advising Through Insights From a Successful Pilot Success Coaching Program
abstract: ABSTRACT Community college student support has historically been a “walk‐in” service. Students identify their needs, connect with a college service, potentially get the assistance they asked for, and leave, often with no follow‐up. This approach is transactional and not proactive, not addressing all the needs students may have or capturing students who might not self‐identify. Waubonsee Community College (WCC) leveraged Title V Grant funding to pilot a success coaching program to provide targeted, in‐time support for students. The gains in student success and retention made in this coaching pilot informed a redesign of advising services to a case management model. This paper explores success coaching and advising structures, the process of an advising redesign to a case management model, and how different positions were leveraged for holistic student support. Data presented include comparisons of student enrollment patterns, gains in continuing and readmitted student enrollment, and the impact on focused populations.

title: Building Capacity at Home: Tribal College Faculty Pursuing Graduate Degrees Through a Reciprocal University Partnership
abstract: ABSTRACT Thirteen Tribal College (TCU) faculty in Montana are pursuing graduate degrees through a reciprocal partnership with Montana State University (MSU) to strengthen TCU capacity and expand local educational opportunities. All TCUs in Montana serve as community colleges for the reservation, are vital to tribal members’ future, and are the academic heart of a community. This paper describes the Tribal College Faculty Pathways program and interviews with participating faculty, framed through the Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT) model with a Cultural Interpretive framework. Three themes emerged: commitment to strengthening the Tribe, dedication to remaining in their Tribal communities, and resilience in overcoming time and financial challenges while developing advanced skills and knowledge as the faculty pursue a graduate education.

title: The Role of the Aspire Alliance's Regional Collaboratives (RCs) in STEM Faculty Pathways
abstract: ABSTRACT This article addresses a critical challenge in postsecondary education: the persistent lack of diversity and limited pathways into STEM faculty roles, particularly at community colleges. We examine how the Aspire Alliance's Regional Collaboratives (RCs) model works to create sustainable two‐year and four‐year partnerships to advance and diversify STEM faculty pathways. The RCs serve as a model for fostering cross‐institutional collaboration and addressing equity gaps in STEM education. By leveraging regional strengths and partnerships, the initiative aims to broaden opportunities for diverse faculty and support systemic change in postsecondary education.

title: Developing and Running a Community College Teaching Fellows Program—Lessons Learned and Insights for Success
abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides a roadmap for four‐year institutions and community colleges to form a regional collaborative, develop and run a community college teaching fellows program, and critically evaluate a program to make year‐over‐year improvements. The case‐study presented focuses on the Central Massachusetts ASPIRE Regional Collaborative (C‐MA RC), bringing together two 4‐year institutions, Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) and Worcester State University (WSU), with a community college, Quinsigamond Community College (QCC), and offers lessons learned and practical guidance from their experience with their teaching fellows program.

title: Centering Relationships, Active Teaching, and Career Development in One STEM Teaching Practicum
abstract: ABSTRACT Broadening participation in STEM fields, particularly among underrepresented minority (URM) groups, has long been a national priority (AIR 2013; The Education Trust 2024). Community colleges—by virtue of their open access, diverse student populations, and teaching‐focused missions—are uniquely positioned to contribute to this effort. The Southern Wisconsin ASPIRE Regional Collaborative (SWARC) leveraged the potential of community colleges to prepare future faculty through an inclusive, mentored teaching practicum. This article outlines the core design principles, implementation strategies, outcomes, and lessons learned from this initiative, with a focus on the role of two‐year institutions in promoting inclusive STEM education and career exploration.

title: Mentored Teaching Practicum Programs as Career Pathways for Future California Community College Faculty in Los Angeles and Orange Counties
abstract: ABSTRACT Teaching practicum programs provide pathways for potential future faculty, such as graduate students and postdoctoral scholars at four‐year universities, to participate in immersive mentorship and professional development experiences at nearby institutions in preparation for a competitive academic job market. These regional initiatives train the next generation of undergraduate instructors and also address an urgent need to hire and retain a diverse, highly trained faculty. This study focuses on a portfolio of mentored teaching practicum programs embedded within the California Community College system in the southern California region, specifically Los Angeles and Orange counties. Using interviews and questionnaires with program leadership and survey data from past participants, this study examines key program features, the benefits and challenges of program implementation, and the impact on program alumni. Findings indicate that these programs share common goals and strategies that lead to participants’ increased interest in and preparation for careers at community colleges.

title: Future Directions Toward Sustainable and Equitable STEM Faculty Pathways
abstract: ABSTRACT This article synthesizes the major themes explored throughout the special issue, highlighting the transformative power of regional collaborations, place‐based innovation, systemic change through collective tools, and reciprocal partnerships in advancing equitable and sustainable STEM faculty pathways. Specifically, the special issue examines how shifting from institutional competition to collaborative ecosystems, honoring local contexts while building national impact, employing structured tools for systemic transformation, and fostering mutually beneficial partnerships can diversify and sustain STEM faculty at community colleges. Ultimately, the authors explore future possibilities in diversifying STEM faculty and continuing collaborative work between two‐year and four‐year institutions.

title: Aspire Regional Collaboratives: A Flexible Model for Cultivating a Diverse and Inclusive STEM Faculty at Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT The Aspire Regional Collaborative (RC) initiative fosters community college and university partnerships that strengthen pathways to STEM faculty positions in community colleges. In this study, we draw from the designing educational innovation for sustained adoption (DEISA) framework to document the progress of the RC initiative. We examine movement across regional collaboratives from “original” to “desired” states across multiple facets, using a mixed‐methods multiple‐case study approach and data from our embedded evaluation team. Our national coalition of RCs also serves as a community of practice working across multiple crucial intersections—organizational change, cross‐institutional partnerships, the professional development of graduate students, and efforts to build a diverse and inclusive STEM faculty. Model adaptation in a region occurs based on the positionalities of RC co‐leads and specific place‐based affordances and constraints. We intend for this manuscript to support stakeholders committed to building a diverse and inclusive STEM faculty, enabling them to adapt the RC model flexibly to their context.

title: Transforming Discourse, Transforming Practice: The Self‐Assessment Tool for Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT Community college faculty remain largely invisible in national data and in tools designed for four‐year institutions. This study uses critical discourse analysis (CDA) to examine how a faculty diversity self‐assessment tool, originally built on Griffin's Institutional Model for Increasing Faculty Diversity for four‐year universities, was adapted for community colleges, attending to the assumptions embedded in its language. Through this critical discourse analysis of the revision process, the study highlights how power and legitimacy are constructed through language, and how university‐centric norms in the original Tool reinforced institutional hierarchies. The adaptation process challenged these discourses by centering teaching‐focused roles, recognizing the diversity and realities of community college faculty, and including issues such as mental health and burnout. The revised tool not only serves as a practical audit for community colleges but also as a discursive intervention to advance faculty diversity and equity and challenge power relations embedded in postsecondary education.

title: Issue Information
Unique Faculty Recruitment in an Era of Postsecondary Change
abstract: ABSTRACT The landscape of postsecondary education is undergoing significant transformation, driven by technological advancement, evolving workforce demands, demographic shifts, and changing student expectations. Community colleges, as engines of workforce development and accessible education, are uniquely positioned at the intersection of these trends. However, the sector faces growing challenges in faculty recruitment due to a shrinking pool of traditional candidates, increased reliance on part‐time and adjunct instructors, and the need for specialized expertise. This chapter traces the historical evolution of enrollment and faculty roles in U.S. higher education, with an emphasis on community colleges’ adaptability to economic and demographic shifts. Special attention is given to the impact of generational changes, labor market competition, and the diversification of both the student body and faculty workforce. The article highlights Ohio's Regional Collaborative as a case study, demonstrating how targeted recruitment of military personnel, veterans, federal civilian employees, and other nontraditional candidates can address faculty shortages. title: Supporting the Shift: Professional Development for Alternative Grading Practices
abstract: ABSTRACT Alternative grading (e.g., contract grading, ungrading, specifications grading) practices have emerged as a promising approach to enhance student success, improve students’ sense of belonging, and make higher education more accessible. This study explores the challenges faced by community college faculty when implementing alternative grading. The authors conducted semi‐structured interviews ( n = 13) with faculty members from a large community college. Study participants represent a diverse range of experience levels and included both part‐time (adjunct) and full‐time faculty. The study revealed that while some instructors are interested in or already practicing some form of alternative grading, they encounter challenges that may hinder widespread adoption. The identified barriers fall into three main categories: (a) affective barriers, (b) structural challenges, and (c) gaps in leadership and collaboration. To address these challenges, the authors argue for the development of comprehensive, ongoing professional development initiatives specifically tailored to community college faculty. These initiatives should go beyond traditional one‐time workshops and instead focus on

title: Issue Information
New Digital Divide in the Age of AI: Equity and Access in Higher Education
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education through personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, and predictive analytics. Despite its potential, uneven implementation risks exacerbating educational inequities, particularly in community colleges, where students are disproportionately from historically underserved populations. This article argues that the AI‐driven digital divide is multifaceted, encompassing disparities in access to technology, AI‐related skills, and equitable outcomes in the design, adoption, and application of AI. Drawing on Van Dijk's digital divide framework, which addresses digital disparities in access, skills, and outcomes, this article examines the intersection of artificial intelligence adoption and equity challenges in community colleges. The discussion underscores how algorithmic bias, faculty preparedness, targeted student support, collaborative partnerships, and inclusive design influence equitable implementation. Drawing on current research and institutional practices, this article proposes actionable, equity‐focused strategies to ensure AI serves as a bridge to opportunity rather than a barrier in community colleges

title: Editor's Note
Strengthening Faculty Development at Tribal Colleges and Universities: A Critical Review and Three‐Tiered Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT Tribal Colleges and Universities (TCUs) play a critical role in Indigenous nation‐building and postsecondary access, yet faculty development within these institutions remains chronically under‐resourced and inconsistently supported. This critical literature review examines faculty development across TCUs that function primarily within the community college sector, with attention to the structural and policy conditions shaping professional growth. Drawing on peer‐reviewed scholarship, institutional data, and cross‐institutional examples, the analysis identifies persistent challenges related to chronic underfunding, faculty workload, limited professional infrastructure, and misalignment between prevailing faculty development models and the missions of Indigenous‐serving institutions. The review synthesizes evidence from 37 TCUs serving approximately 28,000 students annually and examines how faculty development is supported at institutional, consortial, and federal levels. Although TCUs receive substantially less federal funding per student than other public community colleges, the literature documents meaningful innovation in faculty development when culturally grounded appr

title: Learning From Faculty Before Implementing a Culturally Responsive Teaching Program at a Community College
abstract: ABSTRACT Supporting community college faculty with a framework of culturally responsive teaching as a lens through which they can approach their classroom environment is important. Professional development is usually developed and delivered without first learning from faculty about their motivation and current knowledge on the topic. In this article, I describe how a community college first gathered information from faculty before designing and implementing a culturally responsive teaching program. Fourteen community college faculty members at a rural west Texas community college participated in interviews about their teaching experiences and motivations before participating in a six‐week virtual professional development program focusing on culturally responsive teaching. Some had several years of experience working at the college, but most had only been in their positions for less than five years. The study had four major findings. The first was that faculty have a desire to improve their teaching. The interviews showed that faculty who participated in the program did so because they felt a need to change. title: AI‐Driven Faculty Development in an Embedded Community College Model: Balancing Tradition, Innovation, and Inclusivity at UDC
abstract: ABSTRACT This reflective analysis examines faculty development challenges and opportunities at the University of the District of Columbia (UDC), a public HBCU and the only urban land‐grant institution in the United States. As UDC advances a unified “One UDC” vision, the institution is repositioning itself as a flagship university while integrating instruction across multiple locations, including its embedded community college (UDC‐CC), where nearly half of the student population is enrolled. This institutional structure necessitates a coordinated approach to faculty development that supports equity, instructional consistency, and student success across campuses. Drawing on practice‐informed initiatives, the paper describes how AI‐infused faculty development, including live, performative demonstrations using VerseBot, a custom instructional AI persona built on ChatGPT, addresses faculty concerns related to teaching effectiveness, student engagement, academic integrity, and resource disparities. Embedding AI literacy and ethical guidance within first‐year coursework, alongside structured professional development such as Association of College and University Educators (ACUE) certifica

title: Uprooting Traditional Classroom: Belonging, Wellness and Critical Learning Through Community College Nature‐Based Education
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how nature‐based learning (NBL) fosters student engagement, critical observation, mental health, and social belonging at an urban community college. Drawing on over 200 student surveys and qualitative reflections from 14 interdisciplinary, curriculum‐embedded NBL projects, student feedback demonstrates how place‐based pedagogy transforms both learning and relationships. Findings show that integrating nature into class time enhances content retention, reduces stress, and strengthens peer and community connections. This study explores the intersection of mental health and academic outcomes, while centering student voice. By demonstrating how urban campuses can weave nearby green spaces into course design, this work offers a replicable approach for institutions seeking to enhance student well‐being and academic outcomes.

title: Correction to “Demonstrating Care: The Role of Community College Dual Credit Instructors in Supporting Student Success”
Transformation Teams Leading the Hispanic‐Serving Institutions Movement at HSI Community Colleges
abstract: ABSTRACT The Department of Education defunded discretionary grant programs for enrollment‐based minority‐serving institutions (MSIs) on September 10, 2025, yet Hispanic‐serving institutions (HSIs) still exist and must continue to adapt to their growing population of Latine/x students. Hispanic‐serving community colleges (HSCCs) represent 40% of all HSIs, and California is home to the most HSCCs. In this article, we document a participatory action research (PAR) project focused on organizational transformation at two California HSCCs. We outline how Fullerton College and Santa Rosa Junior College engaged in a series of intentional activities, tasks, and processes in order to transform the ways they serve Latine/x students. By implementing HSI Transformation Teams, both campuses created equity‐minded solutions driven by research and data. While the process remains ongoing, this article offers practical recommendations for starting the HSI movement on campus through a collaborative, data‐driven approach.

title: Strengthening Faculty Development Through Cross‐Institutional Partnerships: Assessing Faculty Development Opportunities and Outcomes
abstract: ABSTRACT How can in‐house experts at 2‐year colleges leverage partnerships with colleagues at 4‐year colleges to design, assess, and research faculty development initiatives? This article showcases two examples of Maricopa Community Colleges’ partnership with 4‐year universities: (1) implementation and assessment of the community college district's Literacy Partners Program (LPP) and (2) research on district faculty members’ perceptions of professional development. Drawing on a survey, focus groups, interviews, and critical reflective inquiry, findings suggest that the partnerships led to positive outcomes (e.g., increased use of teaching practices for access and equity, greater understanding of faculty's professional development participation and needs). We conclude this extended example of the community college district's 2‐year/4‐year partnerships in support of faculty development with recommendations for readers pursuing similar partnerships.

title: Assessing a Technology Professional Development Program at a Community College Using the PICRAT Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT Faculty often need support in integrating technology for teaching and learning. This study assesses an in‐house professional development program at a rural Mississippi community college. The program aims to equip faculty with the skills necessary to use digital tools effectively while addressing barriers such as technical difficulties, time constraints, and varying levels of digital proficiency. Data were collected from self‐assessments and project evaluations, focusing on how faculty applied new technology‐based activities in their teaching and the impact on student engagement. The study employed Kimmons et al.’s PICRAT model to assess the level of technology integration in faculty projects. Results indicate that the majority of faculty applied new technology‐based strategies. Additionally, the PICRAT matrix revealed that most projects fell within the “creative amplification” level, suggesting that technology was used to enhance but not radically transform pedagogy.
